lesson.grammar_point: future forms (will, going to, present continuous, future perfect)

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: the ordered set of steps between where you are and where you say you are going
the limit you reach that stops you going further without changing something
the distance ahead that a plan is made for, in years
how wide a job or a project reaches, and where it stops
the written page in which you say what you plan to do and why
to change direction while keeping most of what you have already built
a specific thing you promise to produce, with a date attached to it
happening in small steps rather than in one jump

paras: The first essay reads well. It says the candidate will grow the company, will bring in professional management, and will eventually take the business into new markets. Every sentence is in the future and every one of them is a prediction. Read it twice and you notice that nothing in it has a date, and that nothing in it would have happened by any particular year. It is a horizon with no road map underneath it, and an admissions committee has read four hundred of them this month.

The second essay is duller and it is the one that gets the interview. It says the candidate is applying in October, because the interviews are due to start that month. It says he is going to write the pricing process down whether or not he is admitted, and that this is the first year's deliverable, with a date. It says the change will be incremental, because a company of twenty-five people cannot stop working while its director studies. And it says that by 2029 the site work will have been handed to somebody else, which is a promise about the company rather than about the program.

The difference is not ambition and it is not writing. Both candidates want the same things. The difference is that the second one has separated four kinds of future: what he predicts, what he has decided, what is already in the diary, and what will be finished by a named year. A reader can see, in the verbs alone, how much of the plan exists without the school in it. That is the whole test, and it is decided in the first two paragraphs.

listenings.text: I can tell you in two paragraphs whether somebody has a plan or a wish, and it is not the ambition that gives it away, it is the verbs. An essay written entirely in will is a wish with a date on it. Here is the test I apply to the first goal on every page, and it is not a kind one. Would this still happen if we did not admit you? If nothing on the page survives that question, then the program is being used as the plan, and a program is not a plan. Now, about the long-term goal at the end. Nobody on this side of the table expects it to come true. We are not reading a prediction and marking it right or wrong five years later. What we are reading is whether you can build a road map that connects that goal to something you are doing on Monday morning. If the two ends do not meet, the middle is where you lost us.

I went back and read my own goals essay about a month ago, two years after I wrote it. The long-term goal did not happen. It was never going to happen, and here is the strange part: nobody has ever asked me about it since, not once, not in any conversation. What did matter was the boring paragraph in the middle, the first-year deliverable, which was writing our pricing process down. It was incremental and it was dull and it is the thing that changed the company, because it took the decision out of my head and put it somewhere twenty-five people could see it. If I wrote the essay again today I would put fewer wills in it. I wrote about a future I was predicting, when what the reader wanted was the two or three things I had already decided, with the dates I had already agreed to.
